newsitem.title: USA: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- 5-year TIPS create new curve.
newsitem.headline: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- 5-year TIPS create new curve.

text.p: At last, the much ballyhooed and much maligned U.S. Treasury 10-year index-linked note gets a younger brother.

But the market does not seem ready to pass out cigars at the July 8 debut of five-year Treasury inflation protected securities, better known as TIPS. The Treasury will announce details of the issue Wednesday afternoon.
"I don't think the advent of this second issue is the beginning of an efficient market," said a senior trader who trades TIPS at a primaity dealership.
"The general level of activity has diminished from the second auction," the trader said.

Indeed, the 10-year TIPS was yielding 3.63 percent on Wednesday morning, above its 3.449 percent yield at its inagural auction on January 29 and a touch below 3.65 percent at its second auction on April 8.

Meanwhile, trading volume has been very light, with TIPS volume regularly a fraction of overall 10-year volume. The 10-year TIPS volume Wednesday morning was $38.0 million out of total 10-year volume of $3.5 billion, according to GovPX.
The Treasury said the July 8 five-year note TIPS sale was another step to build up the market and create a yield curve. It will reopen the issue in October and offer a 30-year bond in 1998.

"A 30-year would arguably fill a greater need and provide more useful information to planners and policymakers," said Marc Wanshel, economist at J.P. Morgan & Co. "However, especially in light of the erratic performance of the 10-year TIPS, Treasury would have faced a substantially larger problem marketing an $8.0 billion 30-year issue than an $8.0 billion five-year issue."
Demand for the new five-year TIPS is still sketchy.

"People are still in the discovery process, so the fact there is going to be a yield curve, people will find comfort in that fact," said Scott Graham, co-head bond trader at Prudential Securities Inc.

Traders said they did not wish to speculate about the size of the five-year TIPS, nor would they predict a trading range. But the general feeling was for the Treasury to issue $7.0 billion to $9.0 billion of five-year TIPS that would initially trade 10-15 basis points below the 10-year TIPS. Details will be announced at 1430 EDT/1830 GMT.
"The premium for that (inflation) protection is less (than 10-years)," said Graham. "People who buy five-year don't want exposure to inflation...Therefore, they will play out to a limited audience."
He noted that in the current low inflation environment, investors are not really looking for inflation protection, also evidenced by the fall in gold prices.

"But I think it will generate interest; people will take more chances in this product," Graham said. And, with the Board of Trade coming out with a contract on the TIPS, there will be hedging opportunities, he added.
Another trader cautioned the market not about to give up on these issues just yet.
"It takes a while to build up a marketplace," he said. "The general understanding for dealers and customers takes longer than three auctions."
